modules.summary: This module builds the core skill of computing the surface area of any object made by joining two basic solids. It opens with a catalogue of everyday combined solids — the container-truck, the test tube, domes on buildings — and establishes that such objects are simply joins of the Class IX basics: cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, and hemisphere. The central strategy follows: the total surface area of the new solid equals the sum of the curved surface areas of the exposed parts, never the straight sum of complete TSAs, because the flat faces where the solids meet disappear into the interior. Three worked examples — Rasheed's cone-on-hemisphere top, the cube-plus-hemisphere decorative block, and the cylinder-plus-cone wooden rocket — progressively vary the join pattern (shared face, disc-on-face, unequal-radius ring). Together they teach the student to sketch the join, mark which faces vanish, and add only the exposed surfaces. This readies the student for surface-area word problems in Exercise 12.1 and for the parallel volume work in Modules M2 and M3.

topics.summary: A combined solid is an object built by joining two or more of the Class IX basics — cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, or hemisphere — along matching faces. You spot them everywhere: a container-truck is a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, and a test tube is a cylinder with a hemispherical bottom. For example, Fig. 12.2 shows an oil-tanker whose shape no single basic solid describes, yet the cylinder-plus-two-hemispheres decomposition describes it exactly. Recognising such decompositions is the foundation for every surface-area and volume calculation in the rest of the chapter.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Walk past any Indian village or town and you will pass a dozen objects that mathematics calls ‘combined solids’ — the dome on top of a cylindrical water tank, the hemispherical lid on a brass kalash, the conical roof above a cylindrical shamiana. None of them fits neatly into a single shape from the chapters you studied in Class IX, yet every one of them can be described perfectly by joining two shapes you already know.

RECALL: From Class IX, you are already comfortable with the basic solids: the cuboid, the cone, the cylinder, and the sphere, along with the hemisphere as half of a sphere. You have also learnt how to compute their surface areas and their volumes separately. See Fig. 12.1 in the textbook for a reminder of how each of these shapes looks on its own.

CORE: In our day-to-day life, we come across a number of solids made up of combinations of two or more of the basic solids shown above. You must have seen a truck with a container fitted on its back (see Fig. 12.2), carrying oil or water from one place to another. Is it in the shape of any of the four basic solids mentioned above? You may guess that it is made of a cylinder with two hemispheres as its ends.

Again, you may have seen an object like the one in Fig. 12.3. Can you name it? A test tube, right! You would have used one in your science laboratory. This tube is also a combination of a cylinder and a hemisphere. Similarly, while travelling, you may have seen some big and beautiful buildings or monuments made up of a combination of solids mentioned above.

GROUND IT: Imagine the community drinking-water tank your panchayat installs on a concrete platform — a tall cylinder capped by a hemispherical dome. The same object raises two different questions. When the painter asks how much paint he needs, the answer depends on the exposed curved surfaces. When the panchayat asks how many litres the tank will hold for the village, the answer depends on the combined inside volumes. We will develop the machinery to answer both kinds of questions through this chapter.

CENTRAL QUESTION: If for some reason you wanted to find the surface areas, or volumes, or capacities of such objects, how would you do it? We cannot classify these under any of the solids you have already studied. In this chapter, you will see how to find surface areas and volumes of such objects.

ERROR ALERT: A common first thought is that the surface area of a joined solid is the sum of the complete surface areas of its parts. You will see very soon that this is wrong, because the faces that get glued together disappear from the outside. Hold that thought — we will return to it in the very next section.

CHECK: Before moving on, can you sketch two everyday objects in your notebook — one that is a cylinder plus a hemisphere, and one that is a cone plus a cylinder — from your own kitchen or street?

topics.summary: The total surface area of a combined solid is the sum of only the exposed surfaces of its components, not the sum of their full TSAs. When two solids are joined, the flat circular or flat rectangular faces where they meet disappear into the interior and must be dropped. For example, in an oil-container shaped as a cylinder with two hemispheres at its ends, the two flat circles of the hemispheres vanish at the join, so TSA = 2πrh + 2 × 2πr². This exposed-surface strategy unlocks every surface-area problem on combined solids in the rest of the chapter.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: A container-truck on the highway, a gas cylinder with a rounded cap, a temple dome on a rectangular base — each is two familiar shapes stuck together. Our question is simple: if someone has to paint or wrap such an object, exactly how much surface are they covering?

RECALL: From Section 12.1 you already know that a combined solid is two or more basic solids joined along matching faces. You also already know, from Class IX, the curved surface area (CSA) and total surface area (TSA) formulas for the cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, and hemisphere.

CORE — THE DECOMPOSITION STRATEGY: Let us consider the container seen in Fig. 12.2. How do we find the surface area of such a solid? Whenever we come across a new problem, we first try to see if we can break it down into smaller problems we have earlier solved. We can see that this solid is made up of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck at either end. It would look like what we have in Fig. 12.4, after we put the pieces all together.

If we consider the surface of the newly formed object, we would be able to see only the curved surfaces of the two hemispheres and the curved surface of the cylinder. Notice what is not visible: the two flat circular faces where each hemisphere meets the cylinder have vanished into the interior. They are no longer part of the outside. So, the total surface area of the new solid is the sum of the curved surface areas of each of the individual parts. This gives,

TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere

where TSA, CSA stand for ‘Total Surface Area’ and ‘Curved Surface Area’ respectively.

WHY THIS STEP? We added only CSAs and not TSAs because the flat circular ends of the hemispheres are hidden inside the cylinder and are therefore no longer part of the outer surface. A good habit is to sketch the joined solid and cross out every face that disappears at the join before you write a single formula.

WORKED SET-UP — THE CONE-AND-HEMISPHERE TOY: Let us now consider another situation. Suppose we are making a toy by putting together a hemisphere and a cone. Let us see the steps that we would be going through.

First, we would take a cone and a hemisphere and bring their flat faces together. Here, of course, we would take the base radius of the cone equal to the radius of the hemisphere, for the toy is to have a smooth surface. So, the steps would be as shown in Fig. 12.5.

At the end of our trial, we have got ourselves a nice round-bottomed toy. Now if we want to find how much paint we would require to colour the surface of this toy, what would we need to know? We would need to know the surface area of the toy, which consists of the CSA of the hemisphere and the CSA of the cone. So, we can say:

Total surface area of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone

GROUND IT — THE WEDDING SHAMIANA: Picture the cylindrical-walled, conical-roofed shamiana hired for a village wedding. The contractor bills the family only for the canvas that is actually visible: the curved side of the cylinder and the slanted outside of the cone. The flat circular join where the cone meets the cylinder, and the ground inside the tent, carry no canvas at all. The strategy above gives him exactly the billable area.

ERROR ALERT: Many students initially write 'TSA of combined solid = TSA of shape 1 + TSA of shape 2'. This is wrong because the glued faces are counted twice and they are not even on the outside. The correct strategy is: add the CSAs of every component, then add only those flat faces that remain exposed.

topics.original_chunk:
12.2 Surface Area of a Combination of Solids

Let us consider the container seen in Fig. 12.2. How do we find the surface area of such a solid? Now, whenever we come across a new problem, we first try to see, if we can break it down into smaller problems, we have earlier solved. We can see that this solid is made up of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck at either end. It would look like what we have in Fig. 12.4, after we put the pieces all together.

If we consider the surface of the newly formed object, we would be able to see only the curved surfaces of the two hemispheres and the curved surface of the cylinder. So, the total surface area of the new solid is the sum of the curved surface areas of each of the individual parts. This gives,

TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere

where TSA, CSA stand for ‘Total Surface Area’ and ‘Curved Surface Area’ respectively.

Let us now consider another situation. Suppose we are making a toy by putting together a hemisphere and a cone. Let us see the steps that we would be going through.

First, we would take a cone and a hemisphere and bring their flat faces together. Here, of course, we would take the base radius of the cone equal to the radius of the hemisphere, for the toy is to have a smooth surface. So, the steps would be as shown in Fig. 12.5.

concept_bullets: When two basic solids share a flat face, that face becomes interior and is dropped from the TSA — for example, for a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, TSA = 2πrh + 2 × 2πr², not the sum of their complete TSAs.
The TSA of a cone-plus-hemisphere toy is CSA(cone) + CSA(hemisphere) = πrl + 2πr², because the shared circle at the join is inside.

Before writing any formula, sketch the combined solid and cross out every face that becomes hidden — for example, for a cube with a hemisphere on top, cross out the circle under the dome on the cube's top face.
Adding complete TSAs double-counts the glued faces — for example, naïvely adding TSA(cone) + TSA(hemisphere) would include the shared circle πr² twice.
topics.detailed_summary: The total surface area of a combined solid is the sum of only the exposed surfaces of its components, not the sum of their full TSAs. When two solids are joined, the flat circular or flat rectangular faces where they meet disappear into the interior and must be dropped. For example, in an oil-container shaped as a cylinder with two hemispheres at its ends, the two flat circles of the hemispheres vanish at the join, so TSA = 2πrh + 2 × 2πr². This exposed-surface strategy unlocks every surface-area problem on combined solids in the rest of the chapter.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Rasheed, a Class 10 student, is holding a plain wooden spinning top — a lattu — he received for his birthday. He wants to paint it in bright colours. How much area must his paint cover?

CORE: Example 1 : Rasheed got a playing top (lattu) as his birthday present, which surprisingly had no colour on it. He wanted to colour it with his crayons. The top is shaped like a cone surmounted by a hemisphere (see Fig 12.6). The entire top is 5 cm in height and the diameter of the top is 3.5 cm. Find the area he has to colour. (Take π = 22/7)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• Shape = cone on top of a hemisphere, joined along a common circle.
• Total height of the top = 5 cm.
• Diameter = 3.5 cm, so common radius r = 3.5/2 cm = 1.75 cm.
• π = 22/7.

STRATEGY: Since the cone and hemisphere share a flat circular face (and that face is hidden inside), only the curved surfaces remain exposed.

Solution : This top is exactly like the object we have discussed in Fig. 12.5. So, we can conveniently use the result we have arrived at there. That is :

TSA of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone

STEP 1 — CSA of the hemisphere:
Now, the curved surface area of the hemisphere = ½ (4πr²) = 2πr²
= 2 × (22/7) × (3.5/2) × (3.5/2) cm²

WHY THIS STEP? The full sphere has surface area 4πr², so a hemisphere has exactly half of that, which is 2πr².

STEP 2 — height of the cone:
Also, the height of the cone = height of the top – height (radius) of the hemispherical part
= (5 – 3.5/2) cm = 3.25 cm

WHY THIS STEP? The hemispherical part sticks up by a height equal to its own radius. Subtract that from the 5 cm total, and what remains is the cone’s height.

STEP 3 — slant height of the cone:
So, the slant height of the cone (l) = √(r² + h²) = √((3.5/2)² + (3.25)²) cm = 3.7 cm (approx.)

STEP 4 — CSA of the cone:
Therefore, CSA of cone = πrl = (22/7) × (3.5/2) × 3.7 cm²

STEP 5 — add the two exposed areas:
This gives the surface area of the top as
= 2 × (22/7) × (3.5/2) × (3.5/2) cm² + (22/7) × (3.5/2) × 3.7 cm²
= (22/7) × (3.5/2) × (3.5 + 3.7) cm²
= (11/2) × (3.5 + 3.7) cm² = 39.6 cm² (approx.)

So Rasheed must cover about 39.6 cm² with colour.

ERROR ALERT: You may note that ‘total surface area of the top’ is not the sum of the total surface areas of the cone and hemisphere. The flat bases of the cone and the hemisphere are hidden inside the join, so they must be excluded. Students who add TSA of cone + TSA of hemisphere double-count the hidden circle and inflate the answer.

CHECK: Practise the last step — given that 2πr² and πrl share the common factor πr, rewrite the whole sum as πr (2r + l) and verify it still evaluates to about 39.6 cm². This factored form will save you time in the exercises.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 1.75 cm, l = 3.7 cm, pi = 22/7.
Step 1: factor pi r out: 2 pi r^2 + pi r l = pi r (2r + l).
Step 2: 2r + l = 2(1.75) + 3.7 = 3.5 + 3.7 = 7.2 cm.
Step 3: pi r (2r + l) = (22/7) x 1.75 x 7.2 = (22 x 1.75 x 7.2) / 7 = 277.2 / 7 = 39.6 cm^2.

= 150 – πr² + 2πr² = (150 + πr²) cm²

WHY THIS STEP? – πr² removes the hidden circle; +2πr² adds the exposed dome (because the CSA of a hemisphere is 2πr²). The two terms neatly combine as +πr².

= 150 cm² + (22/7) × (4.2/2) × (4.2/2) cm²
= (150 + 13.86) cm² = 163.86 cm².

CORE: Example 3 : A wooden toy rocket is in the shape of a cone mounted on a cylinder, as shown in Fig. 12.8. The height of the entire rocket is 26 cm, while the height of the conical part is 6 cm. The base of the conical portion has a diameter of 5 cm, while the base diameter of the cylindrical portion is 3 cm. If the conical portion is to be painted orange and the cylindrical portion yellow, find the area of the rocket painted with each of these colours. (Take π = 3.14)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• Total rocket height = 26 cm; cone height h = 6 cm; so cylinder height h′ = 20 cm.
• Cone base diameter = 5 cm, so cone base radius r = 2.5 cm.
• Cylinder base diameter = 3 cm, so cylinder base radius r′ = 1.5 cm.
• π = 3.14.
• r > r′, so the cone overhangs the cylinder — a flat ring of the cone’s base is exposed.

Solution : Denote radius of cone by r, slant height of cone by l, height of cone by h, radius of cylinder by r′ and height of cylinder by h′.

Then r = 2.5 cm, h = 6 cm, r′ = 1.5 cm, h′ = 26 – 6 = 20 cm
and l = √(r² + h²) = √(2.5² + 6²) cm = 6.5 cm

WHY THIS STEP? The slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the cone’s axis and its base radius, so l = √(r² + h²) by Pythagoras — a result you used often in Class IX.

STRATEGY: Here, the conical portion has its circular base resting on the base of the cylinder, but the base of the cone is larger than the base of the cylinder. So, a part of the base of the cone (a ring) is to be painted.

STEP 1 — orange area (cone side + exposed ring):
So, the area to be painted orange = CSA of the cone + base area of the cone – base area of the cylinder
= πrl + πr² – π(r′)²
= π[(2.5 × 6.5) + (2.5)² – (1.5)²] cm²
= π[20.25] cm² = 3.14 × 20.25 cm²
= 63.585 cm²

WHY THIS STEP? πrl is the slanted outer surface of the cone (visible). πr² – π(r′)² is the ring of the cone’s base that extends beyond the cylinder — that ring is also exposed and must be orange. The circle above the cylinder is already hidden, so it is not included.

STEP 2 — yellow area (cylinder side + top ring? no — the cylinder’s top is covered, but its bottom is the only base visible):
Now, the area to be painted yellow = CSA of the cylinder + area of one base of the cylinder
= 2πr′h′ + π(r′)²
= πr′(2h′ + r′)
= (3.14 × 1.5) (2 × 20 + 1.5) cm²
= 4.71 × 41.5 cm²
= 195.465 cm²

WHY THIS STEP? The cylinder’s curved side is fully visible, contributing 2πr′h′. Its top face is hidden under the cone’s base, so it is excluded. Its bottom face is the rocket’s base and is visible, so π(r′)² is added.

ERROR ALERT: Many students automatically add the whole base area of the cone to the orange side. But only the ring π(r² – r′²) — the part that peeks out beyond the cylinder — is exposed. The disc of radius r′ at the centre sits flush against the cylinder top and is hidden. Missing that subtraction is the single most common error in this problem type.

CHECK: Sketch the rocket from directly above. Shade in what you can see — an orange ring around a hidden circle — and write down the formula for just that ring’s area. This visual habit will stop the overlap error before it happens.

segments.summary: This segment builds the surface-area skill from principle to practice. It first establishes the decomposition strategy (T2): the TSA of a combined solid is the sum of the CSAs of its parts, because the flat faces where the solids meet become hidden. Three worked examples then specialise the strategy: Rasheed's top (cone surmounted by a hemisphere, shared circular face, CSA + CSA), the decorative block (hemisphere on a cube, hidden circle subtracted and dome added), and the wooden rocket (cone on a narrower cylinder, producing an exposed ring of the cone's base). Students learn to sketch the join, mark the disappearing faces, and assemble the correct expression before computing.

recall_questions.answer: In Rasheed's top, two entire flat circles of radius r (one from the cone, one from the hemisphere) are hidden, totalling 2 pi r^2 of hidden area. In the decorative block, only one circle of radius r is hidden, because the cube's top face is square and the hemisphere covers just the circular patch of area pi r^2 on it. So Rasheed's top has twice as much hidden area at the join as the decorative block, for the same r. This is why the block's TSA formula gains a net pi r^2 while the top's TSA drops to CSA + CSA only.
recall_questions.prompt: Compare the hidden-face adjustment in the Rasheed's-top problem (cone-plus-hemisphere) with the one in the decorative block (cube-plus-hemisphere). Which solid had more surface area hidden at the join and why?

recall_questions.answer: In Rasheed's top the cone and hemisphere share the same radius, so the full flat circle of each is hidden and both vanish cleanly. In the rocket, the cone's base is larger than the cylinder's top, so only a disc of the cylinder's radius is hidden; the rest of the cone's base is an exposed ring. Hence the rocket's TSA must add the ring area pi (R^2 - r^2) from the cone's base plus the cylinder's bottom circle, which never appears in the Rasheed shortcut. The mismatch in radii is what forces the extra annular term.

modules.brief_summary: This module develops the strategy for finding the surface area of a combined solid as the sum of the exposed curved or flat surfaces of its components, through three varied worked examples.
modules.detailed_summary: This module builds the core skill of computing the surface area of any object made by joining two basic solids. It opens with a catalogue of everyday combined solids — the container-truck, the test tube, domes on buildings — and establishes that such objects are simply joins of the Class IX basics: cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, and hemisphere. The central strategy follows: the total surface area of the new solid equals the sum of the curved surface areas of the exposed parts, never the straight sum of complete TSAs, because the flat faces where the solids meet disappear into the interior. Three worked examples — Rasheed's cone-on-hemisphere top, the cube-plus-hemisphere decorative block, and the cylinder-plus-cone wooden rocket — progressively vary the join pattern (shared face, disc-on-face, unequal-radius ring). Together they teach the student to sketch the join, mark which faces vanish, and add only the exposed surfaces. This readies the student for surface-area word problems in Exercise 12.1 and for the parallel volume work in Modules M2 and M3.
important_points: From Class IX, you are familiar with some of the solids like cuboid, cone, cylinder, and sphere (see Fig. 12.1).
In our day-to-day life, we come across a number of solids made up of combinations of two or more of the basic solids as shown above.
TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere
where TSA, CSA stand for ‘Total Surface Area’ and ‘Curved Surface Area’ respectively.
Total surface area of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone
The top is shaped like a cone surmounted by a hemisphere (see Fig 12.6).
So, the slant height of the cone (l) = √(r² + h²) = √((3.5/2)² + (3.25)²) cm = 3.7 cm (approx.)
So, the surface area of the block = TSA of cube – base area of hemisphere + CSA of hemisphere

Here, the conical portion has its circular base resting on the base of the cylinder, but the base of the cone is larger than the base of the cylinder. So, a part of the base of the cone (a ring) is to be painted.
You may note that ‘total surface area of the top’ is not the sum of the total surface areas of the cone and hemisphere.

modules.summary: This module turns the student from surface-area reasoning to the companion problem of volume, and to real-life applications. Segment M2.S3 closes surface-area work with a bird-bath worked example that yields the memorable factored formula 2πr(h + r), and with Exercise 12.1 where the student practises on nine varied combined solids. Segment M2.S4 introduces the governing volume principle — the volume of a joined solid is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts, because interiors do not vanish at a join the way surfaces do. The principle is then applied in two worked examples: Shanta's cuboid-plus-half-cylinder shed (volumes ADDED, then solid matter subtracted) and the juice-seller's glass with a hemispherical bump (apparent capacity MINUS displaced bump = actual capacity). Together these examples teach the student when volume adds, when it subtracts due to physical hollowing, and how to translate real contexts — sheds, glasses, tanks — into the right sum or difference. This sets up the further volume applications and chapter review in Module M3.

topics.summary: For a cylinder with a hemispherical depression scooped into one end, only the cylinder's curved side and the hemisphere's curved inside are exposed — because the hemisphere's rim sits exactly on the cylinder's rim, no flat circle remains. The total surface area is therefore CSA(cylinder) + CSA(hemisphere) = 2πrh + 2πr², which factors as 2πr(h + r). For example, Mayank's bird-bath with h = 145 cm and r = 30 cm gives 2 × (22/7) × 30 × 175 = 33 000 cm² = 3.3 m². This same factored formula also applies when a hemisphere is mounted on top of a cylinder instead of being scooped in.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Mayank, a bird-lover in Pune, builds a cement bird-bath at the corner of his garden. It is a tall cylinder with a shallow hemispherical scoop carved into its top so that sparrows can drink from it. To waterproof the bath, Mayank must coat every visible surface with sealant — how much surface is that?

CORE: Example 4 : Mayank made a bird-bath for his garden in the shape of a cylinder with a hemispherical depression at one end (see Fig. 12.9). The height of the cylinder is 1.45 m and its radius is 30 cm. Find the total surface area of the bird-bath. (Take π = 22/7)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• A cylinder with a hemispherical depression scooped out of its top face.
• Cylinder height h = 1.45 m = 145 cm.
• Radius (common to cylinder and hemisphere) r = 30 cm.
• π = 22/7.

STRATEGY: Pause and picture what is exposed. The cylinder contributes its full curved side. The hemispherical scoop is carved INTO the top, so the dome of the scoop is now an inward-facing curved surface that is also visible. The original flat circle on top of the cylinder has been replaced by the curved inside of the hemisphere; there is no flat circular rim to count, because the hemisphere’s rim sits exactly on the cylinder’s rim.

Solution : Let h be height of the cylinder, and r the common radius of the cylinder and hemisphere. Then,

the total surface area of the bird-bath = CSA of cylinder + CSA of hemisphere
= 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r)

WHY THIS STEP? Although the hemisphere is cut OUT of the top instead of being placed ON the top, the area of its curved surface is still 2πr² — area does not care which way the curvature faces. The factoring 2πr(h + r) is a useful shortcut you should memorise for cylinder-plus-hemisphere problems.

= 2 × (22/7) × 30 × (145 + 30) cm²
= 33000 cm² = 3.3 m²

ERROR ALERT: A frequent trap is to ADD the flat circular top of the cylinder to the hemisphere’s CSA, thinking the top is still visible. It is not — the circle is literally the boundary of the scoop. Another trap is to SUBTRACT the circle, double-counting its disappearance. Neither happens: the circle simply vanishes, replaced one-for-one by the dome’s CSA.

CHECK: Check your understanding — if Mayank had instead MOUNTED a hemisphere ON TOP of the cylinder (a dome, not a scoop), which surfaces would change? Convince yourself that the formula 2πr(h + r) actually gives the same answer in that other case too, for exactly the same cancellation reason.

Solution : Let h be height of the cylinder, and r the common radius of the cylinder and hemisphere. Then,

the total surface area of the bird-bath = CSA of cylinder + CSA of hemisphere
= 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r)
= 2 × (22/7) × 30 × (145 + 30) cm²
= 33000 cm² = 3.3 m²
concept_bullets: A hemispherical scoop whose rim matches the cylinder's rim leaves no flat circle exposed — the top circle vanishes and is replaced one-for-one by the dome's CSA, so TSA is just 2πrh + 2πr².
Factor the formula as 2πr(h + r) — for Mayank's bird-bath this gives 2 × (22/7) × 30 × 175 = 33 000 cm² quickly.
Always convert heights to a single unit before substituting — Mayank's 1.45 m becomes 145 cm so it matches the radius in cm.
The same formula 2πr(h + r) works for a cylinder with a mounted dome as well — the vanishing-top-circle algebra is identical in both cases.

recall_questions.answer: The TSA counts: the outer CSA of the cylinder, the base circle of the cylinder at the bottom, and the inner curved surface (CSA) of the hemispherical depression. The top circle of the cylinder is hidden because the hemispherical scoop occupies it, so that circle is not counted in the TSA.
recall_questions.prompt: In a bird-bath shaped as a cylinder with a hemispherical depression scooped out of its top, which surfaces contribute to the TSA and which circle is hidden?

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 30 cm, cylinder height h = 1.45 m = 145 cm.
Step 1: CSA of cylinder = 2 pi r h = 2 x (22/7) x 30 x 145 = 191400/7 ~= 27342.86 cm^2.
Step 2: CSA of hemispherical depression = 2 pi r^2 = 2 x (22/7) x 900 = 39600/7 ~= 5657.14 cm^2.
Step 3: base circle of cylinder = pi r^2 = (22/7) x 900 = 19800/7 ~= 2828.57 cm^2.
Step 4: TSA = 27342.86 + 5657.14 + 2828.57 ~= 35828.57 cm^2, i.e., about 3.58 m^2.
recall_questions.prompt: A bird-bath is a cylinder of radius 30 cm and height 1.45 m with a hemispherical depression of radius 30 cm at one end. Find its TSA taking pi = 22/7. Show each step in cm^2.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 14 cm, h = 40 cm, pi = 22/7.
Step 1: CSA of cylinder = 2 pi r h = 2 x (22/7) x 14 x 40 = 2 x 22 x 2 x 40 = 3520 cm^2.
Step 2: CSA of hemispherical depression = 2 pi r^2 = 2 x (22/7) x 196 = 2 x 22 x 28 = 1232 cm^2.
Step 3: base circle of cylinder = pi r^2 = (22/7) x 196 = 22 x 28 = 616 cm^2.
Step 4: TSA = 3520 + 1232 + 616 = 5368 cm^2.
Therefore, the bird-bath's TSA is 5368 cm^2.

HOOK: Every object in these nine problems — cubes joined end-to-end, a capsule, a tent, a hollowed cylinder — is a combined solid. You now have the key tool: decide which faces are exposed, add only those. Let us walk through the full translation strategy for word problems, then turn you loose on the exercise.

RECALL: In T2 and T3–T6 you saw that TSA of combined solid = sum of exposed component surfaces. Some faces disappear at joins (as in Rasheed’s top), some get replaced by curved faces of equal area (as in the bird-bath), and sometimes a ring is added (as in the rocket in Example 3). Every problem below will call for one or more of these three situations.

THE TRANSLATION TEMPLATE — follow it for every problem:

1. THE PROBLEM (in words): read twice. Underline every measurement given.
2. WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: in one sentence, say which basic solids are joined and how (surmounted, mounted, hollowed, joined end-to-end).
3. WHAT DO WE KNOW?: list the given radius, diameter, height, slant height — always convert diameter to radius.
4. WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?: name the exact quantity — TSA, CSA, inner SA, cost, remaining SA.
5. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: draw the solid, shade every exposed face, write the sum.
6. SOLVE: substitute, use π = 22/7 unless told otherwise.
7. CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION: units (cm², m²)? reasonable size? does the cost come out in rupees as expected?

WORKED MICRO-EXAMPLE for Q1 — setting up only, not solving:
• Situation: Two cubes of volume 64 cm³ joined end to end form a cuboid.
• Know: each cube volume 64 cm³, so each edge = ∛64 = 4 cm. Joined edge-to-edge the cuboid is 4 cm × 4 cm × 8 cm.
• Want: surface area of the cuboid.
• Translate: SA = 2(lb + bh + hl) with l = 8, b = 4, h = 4.
• Now finish the substitution yourself and check against the situation.

EXERCISE 12.1

Unless stated otherwise, take π = 22/7.

1. 2 cubes each of volume 64 cm³ are joined end to end. Find the surface area of the resulting cuboid.

2. A vessel is in the form of a hollow hemisphere mounted by a hollow cylinder. The diameter of the hemisphere is 14 cm and the total height of the vessel is 13 cm. Find the inner surface area of the vessel.

3. A toy is in the form of a cone of radius 3.5 cm mounted on a hemisphere of same radius. The total height of the toy is 15.5 cm. Find the total surface area of the toy.

4. A cubical block of side 7 cm is surmounted by a hemisphere. What is the greatest diameter the hemisphere can have? Find the surface area of the solid.

5. A hemispherical depression is cut out from one face of a cubical wooden block such that the diameter l of the hemisphere is equal to the edge of the cube. Determine the surface area of the remaining solid.

6. A medicine capsule is in the shape of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck to each of its ends (see Fig. 12.10). The length of the entire capsule is 14 mm and the diameter of the capsule is 5 mm. Find its surface area.

7. A tent is in the shape of a cylinder surmounted by a conical top. If the height and diameter of the cylindrical part are 2.1 m and 4 m respectively, and the slant height of the top is 2.8 m, find the area of the canvas used for making the tent. Also, find the cost of the canvas of the tent at the rate of ₹ 500 per m². (Note that the base of the tent will not be covered with canvas.)

8. From a solid cylinder whose height is 2.4 cm and diameter 1.4 cm, a conical cavity of the same height and same diameter is hollowed out. Find the total surface area of the remaining solid to the nearest cm².

9. A wooden article was made by scooping out a hemisphere from each end of a solid cylinder, as shown in Fig. 12.11. If the height of the cylinder is 10 cm, and its base is of radius 3.5 cm, find the total surface area of the article.

ERROR ALERT: Problem 2 asks for INNER surface area. Inner means the inside of the hollow vessel — the curved inside of the hemisphere and the curved inside of the cylinder. Do not add the outer surface or the rim. Problem 7 says ‘the base of the tent will not be covered’ — which means you also EXCLUDE the bottom circle of the cylinder. Read each phrase like this one carefully before starting.

CHECK: For each problem, before computing, draw the solid and mark with an X every face that is hidden or excluded. The answer emerges from what is left.

'Inner surface area' of a hollow hemisphere-topped cylinder means only the curved insides — for Q2's vessel of diameter 14 cm and total height 13 cm, inner SA = 2πrh_cyl + 2πr² with h_cyl = 13 − 7 = 6 cm.
When a problem says 'base not covered' (as in Q7's tent at ₹ 500 per m²), exclude the bottom circle — only the cylinder's curved side and the cone's slanted surface are billed.

Hollowing a conical cavity out of a cylinder (Q8) exposes the cone's slant surface from inside and keeps the base disc — TSA = 2πrh + πr² + πrl (the top circle vanishes, the bottom stays, the slant appears).

Given: common r = 7 cm, cylinder height h = 14 cm; bottom circle of cylinder open (not counted); join circle hidden.
Step 1: CSA of hemisphere = 2 pi r^2 = 2 x (22/7) x 49 = 308 cm^2.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 3.5 m, cylinder height h = 4 m, cone slant l = 5 m. No floor.
Step 1: CSA of cylinder = 2 pi r h = 2 x (22/7) x 3.5 x 4 = 88 m^2.
Step 2: CSA of cone = pi r l = (22/7) x 3.5 x 5 = 55 m^2.
Step 3: canvas area = 88 + 55 = 143 m^2.
The flat circle at the cone-cylinder join is hidden, so it is not counted, and there is no floor.

recall_questions.answer:
TSA of a hemisphere = 3 pi r^2, which includes the flat circle of the hemisphere. In a capsule, those two flat circles are hidden at the joins with the cylinder, so they must not be counted.

topics.summary: The volume of a combined solid is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts, unlike surface area where faces at joins vanish. The reason is that interiors merge at a join that is only 2-dimensional, so nothing inside is hidden or removed. For example, a cylindrical water tank capped by a hemispherical dome holds exactly πr²h + (2/3)πr³ litres, with no adjustment. The only time volume is subtracted is when material is physically hollowed out — a conical cavity inside a cylinder, a hemispherical bump pushing into a glass — and even then the subtraction is because real matter has been removed, not because a face disappeared. This additivity rule governs every volume problem in the chapter.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: You have just finished working out surface areas for nine different combined solids. The rule was: carefully SUBTRACT or EXCLUDE the faces that vanish at each join. Volume follows a different — and more forgiving — rule. Nothing ever gets subtracted at a join, because nothing about the INSIDE of a solid is hidden when two solids are fused.

CORE: 12.3 Volume of a Combination of Solids

In the previous section, we have discussed how to find the surface area of solids made up of a combination of two basic solids. Here, we shall see how to calculate their volumes. It may be noted that in calculating the surface area, we have not added the surface areas of the two constituents, because some part of the surface area disappeared in the process of joining them. However, this will not be the case when we calculate the volume. The volume of the solid formed by joining two basic solids will actually be the sum of the volumes of the constituents, as we see in the examples below.

WHY THIS STEP? Surface is a property of the OUTSIDE. When two solids are joined, some outside faces become inside faces — so the outer surface shrinks. Volume is a property of the INTERIOR. When two solids are joined, their interiors simply merge end-to-end, and nothing about the inside is created or destroyed.

So the master rule for the rest of this chapter is:

Volume of combined solid = Volume of part 1 + Volume of part 2 + …

This holds whether the solids are SURMOUNTED (one on top of another) or CARVED / HOLLOWED (one scooped out of another — in which case one of the volumes is SUBTRACTED, not because a face is hidden but because that volume of material has literally been removed).

GROUND IT: Remember the community drinking-water tank from the very first section — a cylinder with a hemispherical dome on top. Its capacity, in litres, is exactly the cylinder’s volume plus the hemisphere’s volume. No adjustment is needed. The same logic applies to the brass kalash on the puja altar: whatever water the stem holds plus whatever water the hemispherical bottom holds is the total capacity — nothing hidden, nothing double-counted.

ERROR ALERT: Students who have mastered the surface-area subtraction rule sometimes carry it over: 'do we subtract the volume where the two solids meet?' No. Two solids meet along a 2-D surface, which has zero volume. There is nothing to subtract. The ONLY time you subtract volumes in this chapter is when material has been physically hollowed out, such as a conical cavity carved into a cylinder.

CHECK: In your notebook, write two headings: 'Surface area — what disappears?' and 'Volume — what disappears?' Under the first, note: flat faces at joins. Under the second, note: nothing (unless material is physically removed). You will use both rules together in every example of this section.

12.3 Volume of a Combination of Solids

In the previous section, we have discussed how to find the surface area of solids made up of a combination of two basic solids. Here, we shall see how to calculate their volumes. It may be noted that in calculating the surface area, we have not added the surface areas of the two constituents, because some part of the surface area disappeared in the process of joining them. However, this will not be the case when we calculate the volume. The volume of the solid formed by joining two basic solids will actually be the sum of the volumes of the constituents, as we see in the examples below.
concept_bullets: Volume of combined solid = V₁ + V₂ + … — for a cylinder-plus-hemispherical-dome water tank, capacity is πr²h + (2/3)πr³ litres.
Surface area subtracts hidden faces; volume does not — two solids meet along a 2-D surface, which has zero volume, so nothing is lost at a join.
Subtraction of volume appears only when real matter is removed — for example, a conical cavity drilled into a cylinder subtracts (1/3)πr²h worth of solid.
The same cylinder-plus-hemisphere shape gives two different sums: CSA(cyl) + CSA(hem) for paint, πr²h + (2/3)πr³ for capacity — inside and outside obey different rules.
topics.detailed_summary: The volume of a combined solid is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts, unlike surface area where faces at joins vanish. The reason is that interiors merge at a join that is only 2-dimensional, so nothing inside is hidden or removed. For example, a cylindrical water tank capped by a hemispherical dome holds exactly πr²h + (2/3)πr³ litres, with no adjustment. The only time volume is subtracted is when material is physically hollowed out — a conical cavity inside a cylinder, a hemispherical bump pushing into a glass — and even then the subtraction is because real matter has been removed, not because a face disappeared. This additivity rule governs every volume problem in the chapter.

recall_questions.answer: The volume of a combined solid is the sum of the volumes of the basic solids that make it up. Every cubic unit of space is counted exactly once, and no volume is hidden or lost at the join.
recall_questions.prompt: State the volume-additivity principle for a combined solid made of two basic solids.

recall_questions.answer: Volume measures the space inside a solid, and the join between two solids is a zero-thickness face that contains no space, so no volume is double-counted or hidden. Surface area, in contrast, measures the outer boundary; the glued faces move inside and stop being part of the outside, so they are removed. That is why the rule for volume is pure addition, whereas surface area requires subtracting the hidden flat faces.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Shanta runs a small textile workshop in a village near Coimbatore. Her shed is shaped like a long rectangular box capped by a half-cylindrical tin roof — the shape you see on every cottage-industry godown across rural India. She has to install a ventilation fan, so she must know how much air the shed actually holds with 20 workers and her machines inside.

CORE: Example 5 : Shanta runs an industry in a shed which is in the shape of a cuboid surmounted by a half cylinder (see Fig. 12.12). If the base of the shed is of dimension 7 m × 15 m, and the height of the cuboidal portion is 8 m, find the volume of air that the shed can hold. Further, suppose the machinery in the shed occupies a total space of 300 m³, and there are 20 workers, each of whom occupy about 0.08 m³ space on an average. Then, how much air is in the shed? (Take π = 22/7)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• Cuboidal body: 15 m long, 7 m wide, 8 m tall.
• Half-cylinder on top: diameter 7 m (so radius 3.5 m), length 15 m.
• Machinery: 300 m³; 20 workers × 0.08 m³ each.
• π = 22/7.

STRATEGY: Apply the master rule of this section — volumes simply add. Find the cuboid’s volume and HALF of a full cylinder’s volume (because only the top half of the cylinder is actually present). Then subtract whatever solid matter occupies the inside.

Solution : The volume of air inside the shed (when there are no people or machinery) is given by the volume of air inside the cuboid and inside the half cylinder, taken together.

WHY THIS STEP? The shed’s interior is the union of two empty regions — the cuboidal hall and the half-cylindrical attic — which share only a 2-D rectangular wall of no volume. So their air-volumes simply add.

Now, the length, breadth and height of the cuboid are 15 m, 7 m and 8 m, respectively. Also, the diameter of the half cylinder is 7 m and its height is 15 m.

So, the required volume = volume of the cuboid + ½ × volume of the cylinder
= [15 × 7 × 8 + ½ × (22/7) × (7/2)² × 15] m³ = 1128.75 m³

Next, the total space occupied by the machinery = 300 m³
And the total space occupied by the workers = 20 × 0.08 m³ = 1.6 m³

Therefore, the volume of the air, when there are machinery and workers
= 1128.75 – (300.00 + 1.60) = 827.15 m³

WHY THIS STEP? The machinery and workers are solid objects occupying the shed’s interior. They are not hidden faces; they are real volumes of matter. Subtract them from the shed’s total volume to find the air that is left.

ERROR ALERT: The half-cylinder’s ‘height’ in the volume formula is the LENGTH of the shed (15 m), not the height above the cuboid. The axis of the cylinder runs horizontally along the roof. Many students mistakenly substitute the 3.5 m ‘dome height’ for the cylinder’s length and lose a factor that matters.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: cuboid 15 x 7 x 8 m; half-cylinder radius r = 7/2 = 3.5 m, length L = 15 m.
Step 1: volume of cuboid = l x b x h = 15 x 7 x 8 = 840 m^3.
Step 2: volume of half-cylinder = (1/2) pi r^2 L = (1/2) x (22/7) x (3.5)^2 x 15 = (1/2) x (22/7) x 12.25 x 15 = 288.75 m^3.
Step 3: total air volume = 840 + 288.75 = 1128.75 m^3.

Given: shed air volume = 1128.75 m^3; each part = 0.6 m^3; 20 parts inside.
Step 1: volume occupied by machines = 20 x 0.6 = 12 m^3.
Step 2: remaining air volume = 1128.75 - 12 = 1116.75 m^3.

topics.summary: When a hollow solid has its interior partly displaced by a bump, apparent capacity (the shape's outer-dimension volume) differs from actual capacity (the liquid volume that actually fits). For a cylindrical glass with a hemispherical bump pushed up from the base, apparent capacity = πr²h, actual capacity = πr²h − (2/3)πr³. For example, a juice-seller's glass with r = 2.5 cm and h = 10 cm has apparent capacity 3.14 × 2.5² × 10 = 196.25 cm³ and actual capacity 196.25 − 32.71 = 163.54 cm³, a loss of about one-sixth of the drink. This subtract-the-bump idea also underlies capacity problems for lassi glasses, chai cups, and similar vessels where material intrudes into the interior.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: A juice seller in Jaipur proudly advertises a ‘large’ glass that is 5 cm wide and 10 cm tall. But the bottom of the glass has a deceptive hemispherical bump rising into it. The customer sees the full cylinder; she actually drinks less. How much less?

CORE: Example 6 : A juice seller was serving his customers using glasses as shown in Fig. 12.13. The inner diameter of the cylindrical glass was 5 cm, but the bottom of the glass had a hemispherical raised portion which reduced the capacity of the glass. If the height of a glass was 10 cm, find the apparent capacity of the glass and its actual capacity. (Use π = 3.14.)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• Cylindrical glass, inner diameter 5 cm → radius r = 2.5 cm.
• Height h = 10 cm.
• Hemispherical bump at the base, same radius r = 2.5 cm, pushes juice out of that region.
• π = 3.14.

STRATEGY: ‘Apparent capacity’ is what the glass would hold if the bottom were flat — the plain cylinder volume. ‘Actual capacity’ is what the glass actually holds: the cylinder minus the hemispherical bump that stole space from the juice.

Solution : Since the inner diameter of the glass = 5 cm and height = 10 cm,

the apparent capacity of the glass = πr²h
= 3.14 × 2.5 × 2.5 × 10 cm³ = 196.25 cm³

But the actual capacity of the glass is less by the volume of the hemisphere at the base of the glass.

WHY THIS STEP? The hemispherical raised portion occupies physical space that juice cannot occupy. Unlike a surface-area subtraction, this is a genuine volume loss — matter literally sits in the way.

i.e., it is less by (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) × 3.14 × 2.5 × 2.5 × 2.5 cm³ = 32.71 cm³

So, the actual capacity of the glass = apparent capacity of glass – volume of the hemisphere
= (196.25 – 32.71) cm³
= 163.54 cm³

ERROR ALERT: Many students treat ‘apparent’ and ‘actual’ as interchangeable words. In mensuration they are not. Apparent capacity is what the outer dimensions would suggest; actual capacity is what liquid actually fits. The gap between them — about 32.71 cm³ here, or a sixth of the drink — is exactly why the same trick appears in lassi glasses, chai cups, and perfume bottles across the country.

CHECK — partially faded: Suppose a cylindrical container of the same 10 cm height has inner diameter 6 cm and a hemispherical bump of the same radius (3 cm) at its base. Set up the expressions for apparent and actual capacity; finish the arithmetic in your notebook and state the difference.

concept_bullets: Apparent capacity is the shape's outer-volume estimate; actual capacity subtracts any material bulging into the interior — for r = 2.5 and h = 10, the gap is (2/3)π(2.5)³ ≈ 32.71 cm³.
Actual capacity = πr²h − (2/3)πr³ for a cylinder with a hemispherical bottom bump — for the juice glass, 196.25 − 32.71 = 163.54 cm³.
The hemispherical bump here is SUBTRACTED (not added) because it is solid material occupying space juice cannot reach — about one-sixth of the drink in this glass.
Always check whether a feature adds to or steals from capacity — a bump pushing UP into the glass steals volume, a bowl scooped DOWN adds volume (as in a bird-bath's reservoir).

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 5 cm, h = 10 cm; hemispherical bump of radius 5 cm at the base.
Step 1: apparent capacity = pi r^2 h = (22/7) x 25 x 10 = 5500/7 ~= 785.71 cm^3.
Step 2: volume of hemispherical bump = (2/3) pi r^3 = (2/3) x (22/7) x 125 = 5500/21 ~= 261.90 cm^3.

segments.summary: This segment introduces the volume-additivity principle and applies it in two worked examples. T8 establishes the rule: because interiors do not vanish at a 2-D join, the volume of a combined solid is simply the sum of its component volumes, with subtraction appearing only when material has been physically removed or displaced. T9 applies the rule to Shanta's cuboid-plus-half-cylinder workshop shed, first adding the two air volumes and then subtracting the machinery and worker occupancy. T10 pushes the rule further with the juice-seller's glass, distinguishing apparent capacity (the full cylinder) from actual capacity (cylinder minus the hemispherical bump at the base). Together the three topics teach the student when to add, when to subtract for hollowing, and how to read a capacity problem critically.

recall_questions.answer: The hemisphere's volume is ADDED when the hemisphere sticks out beyond the other solid; it adds real material or space (e.g., a dome on top of a water tank, where the dome contributes its own (2/3) pi r^3 to the storage). It is SUBTRACTED when the hemisphere is pushed INTO the other solid as a hollow or a raised bump; the material or space of the hemisphere is then missing (e.g., the juice glass of topic T10, where the raised hemispherical base steals (2/3) pi r^3 from the apparent cylindrical volume). The sign depends on whether the hemisphere occupies new space outside or removes space inside.

modules.brief_summary: This module consolidates surface-area word problems from Exercise 12.1 and then introduces the volume-additivity principle for combined solids, applying it to a cuboid-plus-half-cylinder shed and a cylindrical glass with a hemispherical raised bottom.
modules.detailed_summary: This module turns the student from surface-area reasoning to the companion problem of volume, and to real-life applications. Segment M2.S3 closes surface-area work with a bird-bath worked example that yields the memorable factored formula 2πr(h + r), and with Exercise 12.1 where the student practises on nine varied combined solids. Segment M2.S4 introduces the governing volume principle — the volume of a joined solid is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts, because interiors do not vanish at a join the way surfaces do. The principle is then applied in two worked examples: Shanta's cuboid-plus-half-cylinder shed (volumes ADDED, then solid matter subtracted) and the juice-seller's glass with a hemispherical bump (apparent capacity MINUS displaced bump = actual capacity). Together these examples teach the student when volume adds, when it subtracts due to physical hollowing, and how to translate real contexts — sheds, glasses, tanks — into the right sum or difference. This sets up the further volume applications and chapter review in Module M3.

modules.summary: This final module completes the volume programme and consolidates the chapter's two governing principles. In Segment M3.S5, a worked example places a hemisphere-plus-cone toy inside a circumscribing cylinder and computes the toy's volume as (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h, the cylinder's volume as πr²H, and their difference — yielding, in the special case r = h, exactly half the cylinder filled by the toy. Exercise 12.2 then gives the student eight varied volume problems, each demanding a decision between ADD (cone on hemisphere, cylinder with two cones), SUBTRACT (cuboid with conical depressions, cylinder with inscribed toy), DISPLACE (lead shots pushing water out of a cone), and VERIFY (a child's 345 cm³ claim for a spherical vessel). The module closes with a review topic that restates the chapter's two principles side by side: surface area loses faces at joins and must subtract them, volume loses nothing at joins and simply adds. Together the module equips the student with the classification habit — A / S / D / V — that distinguishes the mensuration of a combined solid.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: A solid toy sits on a workshop table — a hemisphere on the bottom and a cone standing on top of it, both sharing the same circular base. A student designer asks: if we slid this toy snugly inside a right circular cylinder that touches the top of the cone and the bottom of the hemisphere, how much empty space would be left inside the cylinder?

CORE: Example 7 : A solid toy is in the form of a hemisphere surmounted by a right circular cone. The height of the cone is 2 cm and the diameter of the base is 4 cm. Determine the volume of the toy. If a right circular cylinder circumscribes the toy, find the difference of the volumes of the cylinder and the toy. (Take π = 3.14)

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
• Hemisphere + cone sharing a common base; diameter 4 cm → r = 2 cm.
• Cone height h = 2 cm.
• Circumscribing cylinder: same radius as the toy’s widest cross-section (r = 2 cm); height equal to the toy’s total vertical extent.
• π = 3.14.

STRATEGY: Use the volume-additivity principle from T8 to get the toy’s volume as (hemisphere volume) + (cone volume). Then find the cylinder’s volume, and subtract.

Solution : Let BPC be the hemisphere and ABC be the cone standing on the base of the hemisphere (see Fig. 12.14). The radius BO of the hemisphere (as well as of the cone) = ½ × 4 cm = 2 cm.

STEP 1 — volume of the toy:
So, volume of the toy = (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h
= [(2/3) × 3.14 × (2)³ + (1/3) × 3.14 × (2)² × 2] cm³
= 25.12 cm³

WHY THIS STEP? The hemisphere’s volume is (2/3)πr³; the cone’s is (1/3)πr²h. The two regions share only a flat circular boundary of zero volume, so nothing is double-counted and nothing is removed — the volumes simply add.

STEP 2 — dimensions of the circumscribing cylinder:
Now, let the right circular cylinder EFGH circumscribe the given solid. The radius of the base of the right circular cylinder = HP = BO = 2 cm, and its height is
EH = AO + OP = (2 + 2) cm = 4 cm

WHY THIS STEP? The cylinder must hug the widest part of the toy, which is the common circle of radius 2 cm, so its radius is 2 cm. Its height stretches from the top of the cone (AO = 2 cm above the base) down to the bottom of the hemisphere (OP = 2 cm below the base), giving 4 cm in total.

STEP 3 — the difference:
So, the volume required = volume of the right circular cylinder – volume of the toy
= (3.14 × 2² × 4 – 25.12) cm³
= 25.12 cm³

Hence, the required difference of the two volumes = 25.12 cm³.

NOTICE: The toy’s volume and the difference both work out to exactly 25.12 cm³ — meaning the toy fills exactly half of the circumscribing cylinder. This is a special feature of the cone-height-equals-radius case; try different heights and the equality breaks.

ERROR ALERT: A classic mistake is to take the cylinder’s height as 2 cm (just the cone height) or 2 cm (just the hemisphere radius) instead of 4 cm (their sum). Always measure the cylinder from the very top of whatever sticks up to the very bottom of whatever hangs down.

CHECK — partially faded: If the same toy were replaced by one with cone height 3 cm (radius still 2 cm), write the new expressions for the toy’s volume and the cylinder’s volume, and finish the arithmetic in your notebook.

The circumscribing cylinder has radius equal to the toy's widest cross-section and height equal to the full vertical extent — here r = 2 cm and H = 2 + 2 = 4 cm, so its volume is π × 4 × 4 = 50.24 cm³.

This exact-half symmetry breaks when cone height changes — for instance, with h = 3 cm the toy's volume becomes (2/3)π × 8 + (1/3)π × 4 × 3 = (28/3)π, no longer half of π × 4 × 5.

The difference is 50.24 − 25.12 = 25.12 cm³ — the toy fills exactly half of the cylinder, a symmetry that holds only when cone height equals radius. This circumscribing-cylinder subtraction is a staple of difficult volume problems.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: These eight problems are your first real test of volume reasoning for combined solids. Some ask you to ADD volumes (cone on a hemisphere, cylinder with two cones). Some ask you to SUBTRACT volumes (conical depressions in a cuboid, a sphere’s displacement of water). One asks you to VERIFY a claim. Each one wants you to decide which it is, using the volume-additivity rule from T8.

RECALL: From T8: Volume of combined solid = sum of component volumes. Material that is physically hollowed or displaced is subtracted; no volume disappears ‘at a join’ the way surface area does. From T9–T11 you have three worked templates: SHED (cuboid + half-cylinder = add), GLASS (cylinder minus hemisphere = subtract displaced material), and TOY-IN-CYLINDER (cylinder minus inscribed solid = subtract).

WHICH-TEMPLATE GUIDE — map each question to a pattern before solving:
• Q1: cone + hemisphere → ADD (like the toy in T11).
• Q2: cylinder + 2 cones → ADD.
• Q3: cylinder + 2 hemispheres → ADD, then take 30 % for the syrup, then multiply by 45 gulab jamuns.
• Q4: cuboid − 4 cones → SUBTRACT (like the glass in T10, but four cavities instead of one).
• Q5: water volume displaced → the dropped lead shots displace water equal to their total sphere volume; solve a ratio equation.
• Q6: cylinder + smaller cylinder → ADD, then multiply by 8 g/cm³ for mass.
• Q7: cylinder − (cone + hemisphere) → SUBTRACT.
• Q8: cylinder (neck) + sphere (body) → ADD and compare with the claimed 345 cm³.

THE TRANSLATION TEMPLATE (same as T7, volume version):
1. THE PROBLEM (in words): read carefully, note the exact quantity asked.
2. WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: name the solids joined or hollowed.
3. WHAT DO WE KNOW?: list radii, heights, diameters — always convert diameter to radius.
4. WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?: volume? mass? number of shots? 30 % of a volume?
5. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: write V = V₁ + V₂ or V = V₁ – V₂.
6. SOLVE using π = 22/7 unless the question says otherwise.
7. CHECK: units (cm³, m³), sensible magnitude, and in Q8 compare against the claimed 345 cm³.

GROUND IT: Picture the wooden pen stand from the stationery shop — a cuboid of 15 cm × 10 cm × 3.5 cm with four little conical holes drilled into it to hold pens. The carpenter pays for wood by volume. He uses exactly (cuboid volume) − (4 × cone volume). That single sentence is Question 4 of the exercise.

EXERCISE 12.2

Unless stated otherwise, take π = 22/7.

1. A solid is in the shape of a cone standing on a hemisphere with both their radii being equal to 1 cm and the height of the cone is equal to its radius. Find the volume of the solid in terms of π.

2. Rachel, an engineering student, was asked to make a model shaped like a cylinder with two cones attached at its two ends by using a thin aluminium sheet. The diameter of the model is 3 cm and its length is 12 cm. If each cone has a height of 2 cm, find the volume of air contained in the model that Rachel made. (Assume the outer and inner dimensions of the model to be nearly the same.)

3. A gulab jamun, contains sugar syrup up to about 30% of its volume. Find approximately how much syrup would be found in 45 gulab jamuns, each shaped like a cylinder with two hemispherical ends with length 5 cm and diameter 2.8 cm (see Fig. 12.15).

4. A pen stand made of wood is in the shape of a cuboid with four conical depressions to hold pens. The dimensions of the cuboid are 15 cm by 10 cm by 3.5 cm. The radius of each of the depressions is 0.5 cm and the depth is 1.4 cm. Find the volume of wood in the entire stand (see Fig. 12.16).

5. A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone. Its height is 8 cm and the radius of its top, which is open, is 5 cm. It is filled with water up to the brim. When lead shots, each of which is a sphere of radius 0.5 cm are dropped into the vessel, one-fourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped in the vessel.

6. A solid iron pole consists of a cylinder of height 220 cm and base diameter 24 cm, which is surmounted by another cylinder of height 60 cm and radius 8 cm. Find the mass of the pole, given that 1 cm³ of iron has approximately 8g mass. (Use π = 3.14)

7. A solid consisting of a right circular cone of height 120 cm and radius 60 cm standing on a hemisphere of radius 60 cm is placed upright in a right circular cylinder full of water such that it touches the bottom. Find the volume of water left in the cylinder, if the radius of the cylinder is 60 cm and its height is 180 cm.

8. A spherical glass vessel has a cylindrical neck 8 cm long, 2 cm in diameter; the diameter of the spherical part is 8.5 cm. By measuring the amount of water it holds, a child finds its volume to be 345 cm³. Check whether she is correct, taking the above as the inside measurements, and π = 3.14.

ERROR ALERT: Q5 is a DISPLACEMENT question, not an addition question. Each lead shot pushes an amount of water equal to its own volume out of the cone. The number of shots is (water displaced) ÷ (one shot’s volume). Q8 is a VERIFY question — your job is to report whether 345 cm³ matches, not to accept it.

CHECK: Before touching any calculator, write next to every question number one of the letters A (add), S (subtract), D (displace), or V (verify). This meta-step is where the actual learning happens.

Given: r = 1.4 cm, cylinder length = 2.2 cm; 45 sweets; syrup fraction = 30 percent.

= (22/7) x 1.96 x (2.2 + 1.867) = (22/7) x 1.96 x 4.067 ~= 25.05 cm^3.

topics.summary: The chapter is governed by two contrasting rules for combined solids. For surface area, add only the exposed surfaces — the curved sides of all parts plus any flat faces that remain visible — and drop every face that gets hidden at a join. For volume, simply add the component volumes, because interiors do not vanish at 2-D joins; subtract only when material is physically removed or displaced. For example, a cone-on-hemisphere toy has TSA = πrl + 2πr² (the shared circle is hidden) but volume = (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h (no adjustment at the join). Keeping these outside-versus-inside rules separate is the single most important habit the chapter builds.
